content: Cerivastatin was once considered the most potent statin available, but it was withdrawn from the market due to fatalities caused by rhabdomyolysis. The specific dose-related effects of cerivastatin on blood lipids, however, remain unclear. The primary objective of this review was to quantify the effects of various doses of cerivastatin on surrogate markers such as LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides in both children and adults, regardless of the presence of cardiovascular disease. The review aimed to characterize the dose-dependent effects and variability of cerivastatin on these markers. Secondary objectives included assessing the impact of cerivastatin doses compared to placebo on withdrawal rates due to adverse effects and comparing its potency to other statins, including fluvastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin, in terms of lipid-lowering effects. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to March 2019. Additional sources such as the European Patent Office, FDA.gov, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses were also searched. Authors of relevant studies were contacted for further published and unpublished data. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled before-and-after studies that evaluated the dose-response effects of fixed doses of cerivastatin on blood lipids over a period of three to 12 weeks. Participants of any age, with or without cardiovascular disease, were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted data. Data from RCTs and controlled before-and-after studies were entered into Review Manager 5 as continuous and generic inverse variance data, respectively. Information on withdrawals due to adverse effects was collected from the RCTs. The risk of bias in the included trials was assessed using categories such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential biases. A total of 50 trials, including 19 RCTs and 31 before-and-after studies, were analyzed. These trials involved 12,877 participants who had their LDL cholesterol levels measured. The participants included individuals of all ages, with and without cardiovascular disease, and the treatment duration ranged from three to 12 weeks. Cerivastatin doses ranging from 0.025 mg/day to 0.8 mg/day resulted in LDL cholesterol reductions of 11.0% to 40.8%, total cholesterol reductions of 8.0% to 28.8%, and triglyceride reductions of 9.0% to 21.4%. The certainty of evidence for these effects was judged to be high. Log dose-response data for doses between 2.5 mg and 80 mg demonstrated strong linear dose-dependent effects on LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and triglycerides. When compared to other statins, cerivastatin was found to be approximately 250 times more potent than fluvastatin, 20 times more potent than atorvastatin, and 5.5 times more potent than rosuvastatin in reducing LDL cholesterol. Similarly, it was 233 times more potent than fluvastatin, 18 times more potent than atorvastatin, and six times more potent than rosuvastatin in reducing total cholesterol. For triglycerides, cerivastatin was 125 times more potent than fluvastatin, 11 times more potent than atorvastatin, and 13 times more potent than rosuvastatin. However, cerivastatin did not exhibit a dose-related effect on HDL cholesterol, although it increased HDL cholesterol by an average of 5%. The risk of bias for lipid measurements was low, but there was a high risk of bias for the outcome of withdrawals due to adverse effects. In 11 out of 19 short-term trials, there was no significant difference in withdrawal rates due to adverse effects between cerivastatin and placebo (risk ratio 1.09, 95% confidence interval 0.68 to 1.74). In conclusion, the lipid-lowering effects of cerivastatin on LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and triglycerides were linearly dependent on dose. The log dose-response data for cerivastatin were linear across the commonly prescribed dose range. Compared to fluvastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin, cerivastatin demonstrated significantly greater potency in reducing LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and triglycerides. However, the review did not provide a reliable estimate of the incidence of adverse effects associated with cerivastatin due to the short duration of the trials and the lack of adverse effect reporting in 42% of the RCTs.
